headline: Prompt injection exploits enterprise AI's design flaws, impacting agents & RAG
summary: Cybercriminals are leveraging prompt injection to steal credentials and cryptocurrency by manipulating enterprise AI systems, with OWASP ranking it the top LLM vulnerability.
details: Prompt injection remains a critical threat to enterprise AI, identified as LLM01 by OWASP for the second consecutive year. This vulnerability arises because LLMs struggle to reliably distinguish between instructions and data, making them susceptible to manipulation through crafted inputs.

CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report revealed that malicious prompts were injected into generative AI tools at over 90 organizations in 2025, leading to the theft of credentials and cryptocurrency. The report emphasizes that AI-enabled adversaries increased their attack volume by 89%, with prompt injection serving as both an entry point and a force multiplier.

Real-world incidents highlight the severity of these attacks. In August 2024, a vulnerability in Slack AI allowed attackers to exfiltrate data from private channels. More recently, in June 2025, a zero-click prompt injection exploit against Microsoft 365 Copilot (EchoLeak, CVE-2025-32711) enabled attackers to access and transmit internal file contents with a single crafted email.

These prompt injection techniques have evolved to target multi-agent architectures, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, model routers, and long-term memory capabilities. Attackers exploit the difficulty LLMs face in separating instructions from data to manipulate model behavior, corrupt outputs, and propagate malicious information through AI systems.

The risk extends beyond mere model misbehavior. Attackers can embed malicious code in documents ingested by RAG pipelines, override previous instructions, or even permanently reconfigure LLM states through long-term memory manipulation. Model routers are also targeted, with attackers forcing prompts to the weakest or least-guarded LLM.

To mitigate these risks, organizations must treat all external data, including RAG sources, as potentially hostile. Implementing robust security measures to prevent RAG pipelines from ingesting poisoned external content is crucial for safeguarding AI deployments.
